passage: At the fair week of the village temple, Charu handed out prasad and steel cups of buttermilk from the back of the hall. She had done it for three years and liked how the day fell into a rhythm. This year the committee head, Lavanya, announced that each volunteer family should give a fixed sum for the new gate, and that donors' names would be read out on the loudspeaker. Charu did the sums in her head: her father's tailoring shop had had a slow winter. She said quietly, "Lavanya akka, I can give my hours, but not that amount." Lavanya frowned, then softened. "Then give hours. Wash the vessels with the boys." Later a family from the next village, not regulars, hesitated at the door. Charu waved them in and pressed a cup into the mother's hand.

qa.q: What did the committee head announce for each volunteer family?
qa.a: Lavanya announced that each volunteer family should give a fixed sum for the new gate, and that donors' names would be read out on the loudspeaker.

qa.q: What was Charu worried about when she did the sums in her head?
qa.a: Charu worried about affording the fixed sum, since her father's tailoring shop had a slow winter, and did not want to be pushed beyond her means.

qa.q: How did Charu handle the pressure to give?
qa.a: She calmly offered her hours instead of the sum, so she could keep serving without going beyond her means.

qa.q: How might the family from the next village feel when X
qa.a: Possibly welcomed and relieved, since the service seems meant to be open to everyone.

grounding: Charu finds meaning in serving at the temple, gives time rather than the pressured sum, and welcomes strangers.

passage:
Kitchen coordinator's note, Sunday langar

Payal came in at five again today, before the dal was even soaked, and stayed through the last round of washing. That is her third double shift this month. She moves fast, laughs with the aunties at the rotis, and quietly seats the construction workers from the site next door when they hesitate at the gate.
At the tea break I saw Vinita, from the committee, telling her that 'real sevadars' sponsor a full day's meal and get their family name read out. Payal's smile went stiff. She said she'd think about it.
Afterwards I sat with her on the steps. I told her the kitchen needs her hands more than her money, that nobody's name is read out for washing pots, and that she can say no. She let out a long breath and said she'd been lying awake over it.

qa.q: How many double shifts had Payal done that month?
qa.a: It was her third double shift that month.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling after Vinita spoke to her about sponsoring a meal?
qa.a: She felt pressured and uneasy; her smile went stiff, and later she admitted she had been lying awake over it.

qa.q: How did the coordinator support Payal, and why did it matter?
qa.a: They sat with her, told her the kitchen needs her hands more than her money, and made clear she could say no, which took away the pressure to give beyond what she could.

qa.q: How might the construction workers experience Payal seating them at the langar?
qa.a: They may feel welcome instead of unsure, because she noticed them hesitating at the gate and made space for them to eat like anyone else.

grounding: A young volunteer finds meaning in serving at a community kitchen, is pressured to give for status, and an adult reminds her that service need not go beyond her means.

passage:
Sunday. Late.

Annadanam day at the temple. I was on the rice counter from eleven, ladling onto banana leaves till my wrist ached. Best ache of the week, honestly.
Pooja aunty caught me at the tap. "Dhruv beta, you've been coming every Sunday for a year. We'll put your name on the donor board, near the entrance."
I said no thanks. I haven't donated anything; I just serve rice. She looked a bit hurt, like I'd refused a gift.
Then a man in a cap stood at the edge of the hall, not sure if he could sit. He asked me, quietly, "Anyone can eat here?" I said yes, and put a leaf down for him next to a group of college boys.
That moment beat any board. I want to keep it this way: I show up, I serve, nobody has to know my name.

qa.q: What was Dhruv doing at the temple from eleven?
qa.a: He was on the rice counter, ladling rice onto banana leaves.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv feel uncomfortable about having his name on the donor board?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and a little embarrassed, because he had only served rice, not donated, and he wanted his service to stay quiet rather than bring him status.

qa.q: What could Dhruv say to Pooja aunty next time so she does not feel brushed off?
qa.a: He could thank her warmly for noticing him and explain that serving without a name on the board is what gives him joy.

qa.q: How might the man in the cap see Dhruv's answer?
qa.a: He probably felt relieved and welcomed, since he was unsure he was allowed to eat until Dhruv said yes and set a leaf down for him.

grounding: A young man finds meaning in serving food at his temple, turns down public recognition, and makes sure a stranger feels the meal is open to all.
